title: What's the deal with Stradivarius violins?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Stradivarius violins: the origins of the violin in sixteenth-century Italy and its rise in respectability after Catherine de Medici's order, the Amati family of Cremona, the design of the violin body and parts, Antonio Stradivari's life, career and golden period, his famous instruments such as the Messiah, the modern theories on why his violins sound so good (Little Ice Age spruce, Joseph Nagyvary's varnish hypothesis, the "it was just him" view), their enormous auction prices, the flood of fakes labeled Stradivarius, and a listener email from Becks Bloomfield.
topics: Little Ice Age violin wood theory

segments.title: Opening banter and fiddle chat
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Josh's violin and other instruments he has bought but not learned, then introduce the topic of the fiddle and violin.

segments.title: Origins of the violin and the Amati family
segments.summary: The fiddle was initially a disreputable tavern instrument in the sixteenth century, until Catherine de Medici ordered thirty-eight violins from Nicolo Amati in 1564. The Amatis of Cremona are described as the de facto inventors of the violin, cello and viola, making Cremona the center of violin production.

segments.title: Violin design and parts
segments.summary: The curves of the violin body are said to produce even resonance across notes, and the C-bouts let the bow reach the strings. The hosts describe the parts: scroll, neck, fingerboard, f-holes, bridge, tailpiece and chin rest. They also note how hard violin playing is compared with guitar.

segments.title: Antonio Stradivari's early career
segments.summary: Stradivari apprenticed under Nicolo Amati, according to his 1666 label, though some suggest the claim was a career move. He built violins in his attic, moved house in 1680, and by 1684 was regarded as Cremona's best maker. He also made cellos, guitars, mandolins and harps.

segments.title: Stradivari's design changes and varnish
segments.summary: Stradivari altered the design with straighter C-bouts, straighter and longer f-holes, a larger scroll and a stronger bout, and developed his own deep red-brown varnish. The hosts say his violins are still considered the best, and a quote compares knockoffs to a school bus versus a Ferrari.

segments.title: Golden period, the Messiah, and his later years
segments.summary: Stradivari's golden period ran roughly from 1700 to 1725. The Messiah, made in 1716, was never sold and stayed in his workshop. His eyesight and hands declined after the golden period, but he kept working into his nineties. About 650 of his roughly 1,100 instruments survive, and many are named after famous owners.

segments.title: Playing, breaking in and wood aging
segments.summary: Violinists believe a violin takes on the character of its players, and that it sounds better the more it is played. The hosts compare this to breaking in jeans and note that the fingerboard and frets wear in.

segments.title: Theories on why Stradivarius violins sound great
segments.summary: Old myths included soaking wood in salt water and volcanic ash coatings; Dragon's blood in the varnish is mentioned. Modern theories include the Little Ice Age producing more uniform spruce, which was undermined because other makers had the same wood. Joseph Nagyvary of Texas A&M proposed that a chemical varnish weakened the wood, which drew pushback. Violinist James Ehnes says there are a thousand factors.
topics: Little Ice Age violin wood theory

segments.title: Auction prices, fakes, and authentication
segments.summary: Stradivarius violins sell for millions of dollars, with the figures reported inconsistently. The Messiah is held by the Ashmolean at Oxford and is considered priceless. Many fakes were made in Germany and Czechoslovakia, some labeled with Stradivari's name. Appraisers receive many calls, and only about 650 instruments are known to exist.

segments.title: Stolen and misplaced Stradivarius violins
segments.summary: A famous Stradivarius was stolen decades ago from a concert violinist and found in a Milwaukee attic. Joshua Bell reportedly left his Stradivarius in a New York cab and later had to play on a cheap fiddle.

segments.title: Listener mail from Becks Bloomfield
segments.summary: A listener praises Chuck's comments on women in science and raising children, from the steam episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, share social media handles and website, and sign off.
